claims.text: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy has a fine lamellar FCC/B2 microstructure.
The FCC lamellae are relatively soft and the B2/intermetallic lamellae are relatively hard.
An oxidizing environment promotes oxide-film formation, unlike an inert or ultra-high-vacuum environment.
Elevated-temperature sliding produces dynamic cycles of oxide formation and removal.
The constituent phases have different chemistry and mechanical properties at their boundaries.
Phase-to-phase differences cause differential oxidation and mechanical stability at the lamellar interfaces.
A thin protective oxide forms on both phases at elevated temperature.
Sliding wear selectively removes the protective oxide at phase boundaries.
Oxide removal exposes fresh, chemically active phase-boundary surfaces.
Galvanic differences between the phases cause preferential corrosion of the exposed interfaces.
Repeated oxide removal and interfacial corrosion synergistically accelerate both wear and corrosion.
Combined wear-corrosion produces significantly greater total material loss than either isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
The wear rate under combined exposure is higher because repeated disruption prevents a robust protective oxide from persisting.
The corrosion rate under combined exposure is elevated at phase boundaries.
Combined exposure produces localized deep-penetration corrosion that is less prominent under isolated exposure.
The mechanism applies when oxidation is sufficient to form a moderately protective film and wear is sufficient to disrupt it without independently causing wholesale mechanical failure.
A thicker, more stable pre-formed oxide at phase boundaries should reduce total degradation, wear, and localized corrosion during otherwise identical combined testing.
Phase-boundary chemistry and lamellar scale may alter the intensity of wear-corrosion coupling.
